title: The Pilgrimage to Samanta-panchaka
story:
In the middle of the day, the sun went dark over Dwaraka — and Krishna's people did not read the eclipse as a bad omen. A solar eclipse, everyone knew, was a summons, not a warning: a day when the pious go down to the holy waters, bathe away the dust of their years, and give cows and gifts to the worthy. Every family in the city knew what such a day demanded — the dark sun above, the sacred water ahead, and blessings to be won by those who came with open hands.

The road led to Samanta-panchaka, the field of the Kurus. Long ago, the old verses say, the warrior-sage Parashurama — a Rama of an age long past, the best of all weapon-bearers — had brought the kings of the earth low on that very field, and the five pools he left behind were called Rama's pools, their water counted among the holiest in the land. Krishna went, and his elder brother Balarama, and his father Vasudeva, and Akrura, the wise elder of the clan, and the chief men of the Yadava houses — and behind them half the city of Dwaraka. The road filled with chariots that gleamed like the dwellings of the gods, drawn by swift horses and hung with garlands of gold, so that the whole procession shone as it crossed the plain beneath the darkened sky. It seemed that all the people of the land were on the road too, streaming toward the same field, each pilgrim hoping to leave a lifetime of wrongs behind in the sacred water.

At the field they bathed in Rama's five pools, fasting with their minds gathered close, and then, as the rite required, bathed a second time. They gave cows and gifts, and did all that the day asked of them. And only then did the field show them what the eclipse had truly gathered.

Kings had come from every quarter — from Kamboja and Kaikaya, from Madra and Kunti, from Anarta and Kerala — and with them, kinsmen and friends the Yadavas had not seen in years. Men parted by wars and reigns and the long business of kingdoms fell on one another's necks, their faces opening like lotuses in the joy of meeting, tears running down unchecked. The women of the two houses embraced as well, arm crossing arm, the red festival powder called kumkuma marking each other's shoulders, tears of love bright in their eyes. The youngest bowed to the eldest and were blessed in return, and the elders gave the blessings with both hands, as if they could not let go.

By evening the field had become something rarer than a festival: half the world's families finding one another again. Tents had risen everywhere; the plain was a city of its own. Old quarrels were forgotten at the sight of a familiar face. News was exchanged at every campfire; children born since the last meeting were shown to relatives who wept over them; men who had last met on a battlefield found they could laugh together. The eclipse that had darkened the noon sky had become the excuse for a homecoming no one had dared to arrange.

And then, toward the end of the day, a new dust rose on the road — not the thin dust of chariots but the slower, thicker dust of ox-carts and walking herds. A caravan of cowherds came up out of the haze, men in the rough cloth of the countryside, and a stir ran through the Yadava camp. For among all the kings and kinsmen the field had gathered, these were the faces from the oldest years of Krishna's life: Nanda, the cowherd chief who had raised him, and Yashoda, who had been a mother to him, with the cowherds of Gokula, the village of his boyhood, around them.
reflection: The eclipse gathers what the years have scattered: a day that begins in darkness becomes the occasion for half the world's families to find one another again. Krishna travels to the tirtha like everyone else, and the story's weight falls not on anything he does but on the reunion that his presence draws together.
next_story_tease: Nanda and Yashoda had come to Samanta-panchaka — and the Vrishnis rushed to meet them as if life itself had returned.
hero_scene: Under the eclipsed sun, a long procession of golden chariots crosses the plain toward the five pools of Samanta-panchaka, where kings from many realms and long-separated kinsmen embrace one another with tears of joy.
